SIM Lab · KFUPM

Sustainable Interfaces
and Membranes

Polymer membrane fabrication, interfacial engineering and selective transport.

SIM Lab investigates the relationships between membrane formulation, interfacial chemistry and separation performance. Based in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at KFUPM, the group develops and evaluates membrane materials for water treatment, desalination-related separations and wastewater processing.

About

Introduction

Sustainable Interfaces and Membranes at KFUPM.

The Sustainable Interfaces and Membranes Laboratory (SIM Lab) is based in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Dhahran, Saudi Arabia. Led by Dr Muhammad Irshad Baig, the group studies membrane materials, aqueous fabrication and interfacial chemistry for water and wastewater separations.

The group includes postdoctoral researchers, doctoral and master’s students, and undergraduate researchers. Its work combines materials preparation with analysis of membrane structure, surface chemistry and transport. Experimental characterization is supported by group activities and shared KFUPM infrastructure.

Sustainability in membrane research

Aqueous phase separation replaces the organic casting medium with water in the reported PEC membrane systems. This changes solvent use during fabrication, but a complete environmental assessment must also account for pH adjustment, salt consumption, washing, crosslinking and membrane lifetime. A water-based casting step alone does not establish the environmental performance of the full process.

Water-treatment and materials research are relevant to the United Nations goals for clean water and sanitation and responsible consumption and production. These links describe the research context, rather than a quantified societal or environmental outcome.

Membrane Science

Understanding membranes: from selective barriers to separation technology

An introduction to selective transport, membrane fabrication and separation processes, with emphasis on the relationship between material structure, operating conditions and performance.

Separation is an essential part of producing clean water and useful chemicals. A feed stream may contain valuable components, unwanted contaminants, or both. A membrane provides a selective pathway through which these components move at different rates. The aim is not always to remove everything: it may be to retain a product, recover a resource, or produce a stream with a specified composition. This makes membrane technology relevant to water treatment, manufacturing, biotechnology, and energy systems.

In this article

  1. Membrane function and architecture
  2. Transport mechanisms and selectivity
  3. Membrane fabrication and structure formation
  4. Water treatment and reverse osmosis

  7. Process integration and sustainability

Membrane function and architecture

A membrane is a material that separates two regions and restricts the movement of certain components relative to others. The incoming mixture is the feed. Material crossing the membrane forms the permeate; the stream remaining on the feed side is the retentate, sometimes called the concentrate. These terms describe the streams, not their quality: depending on the application, either stream can be the desired product.

A membrane should therefore not be understood simply as a very fine sieve. Some membranes contain interconnected pores that admit water while retaining larger particles. Others have a dense selective layer in which molecules interact with the material and move through its molecular-scale structure. A porous support can provide mechanical strength while a much thinner surface layer provides most of the selectivity. This separation of functions is central to thin-film composite membrane design. [2]

Transport mechanisms and selectivity

Transport requires a driving force. Depending on the process, this may be a difference in pressure, concentration, electrical potential, or temperature. More generally, the membrane permits transport in response to differences in chemical potential. Selectivity arises because the components do not respond to the membrane in exactly the same way. [3]

In porous filtration membranes, size exclusion is important: a particle or macromolecule may be too large to enter the available pores. Surface charge and interactions with the pore walls can also influence rejection. For dense polymeric membranes, the classical solution–diffusion model describes transport through preferential sorption into the polymer followed by diffusion across it. A gas can therefore permeate quickly because it dissolves readily, diffuses rapidly, or both. The appropriate model depends on the material and process; no single picture describes every membrane. [3]

Membrane fabrication and structure formation

Fabrication establishes the connectivity of the membrane framework, the properties of its feed-facing surface and the distribution of transport resistance. Three fabrication concepts illustrate different ways of controlling these structural features; they are alternative approaches rather than sequential stages of a single process.

Nonsolvent-induced phase separation

In nonsolvent-induced phase separation, a polymer is dissolved in a suitable solvent and cast as a film or spun as a hollow fibre. Contact with a nonsolvent bath causes exchange between the casting solution and the bath. The mixture demixes, and a polymer-rich phase solidifies into the membrane framework. Polymer concentration, solvent choice, additives, bath composition, and exchange rate influence the resulting skin, pores, and support structure. A change in formulation can therefore change permeability, strength, and rejection even when the polymer itself remains the same. [4]

Aqueous phase separation and polymer ionization

Selected polyelectrolytes can be processed in water by controlling their charge and interactions. In pH-shift aqueous phase separation, a change in pH can promote complexation between oppositely charged polymers and precipitate a water-insoluble network. Mild pH-shift fabrication has been demonstrated for poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate), or PSS, and polyethyleneimine, or PEI. Casting conditions and coagulation chemistry help determine whether the resulting structure is suitable for a particular separation. Water-based processing is promising, but its sustainability still depends on the complete formulation and manufacturing process. [5]

For this polymer pair, the pH response is associated with the ionization of the weakly basic PEI component. Increasing its protonation promotes association with anionic PSS. The resulting membrane is a hydrated polyelectrolyte complex, rather than simply a mechanically filtered mixture of the two polymers. The extent of association, network hydration and conditions of solidification influence the structure available for subsequent transport. The designation “aqueous” identifies the processing medium; it does not imply a unique pore size or a universal level of salt rejection.

Interfacial polymerization and composite membranes

A common route to a thin-film composite membrane is to bring reactive monomers together at the boundary between two phases. For many desalination membranes, an amine and an acyl chloride react to form a thin polyamide layer on a porous support. The support must allow transport without losing mechanical integrity; the selective layer must remain continuous and resist defects. Its chemistry, thickness, and crosslinking influence water transport and solute rejection. [2]

This architecture allows the selective layer and the supporting structure to be optimized for different functions. However, they do not operate independently: the support influences wetting and monomer uptake during fabrication, while its hydraulic resistance contributes during filtration. The introduction of a nanofiller creates a thin-film nanocomposite only when an additional material is incorporated into the relevant composite structure. A filler is not automatically beneficial; aggregation or interfacial defects may increase transport while reducing selectivity.

Water treatment and reverse osmosis

Water-treatment processes are selected according to what must be separated. Microfiltration and ultrafiltration are used to retain suspended particles, colloids, and larger biological or organic components. They do not ordinarily remove dissolved salts effectively. Nanofiltration provides tighter molecular and ionic separation; rejection depends on solute size, charge, membrane chemistry, and feed conditions. These processes may serve as pretreatment or as individual treatment steps. [1]

Reverse osmosis (RO) is used when substantial dissolved-salt removal is required. Water naturally tends to move toward a more concentrated solution by osmosis. In RO, an applied pressure exceeding the opposing osmotic-pressure difference drives water in the desired direction through the selective layer, producing a lower-salinity permeate and a more concentrated brine. Seawater desalination is an important example, but the same principle is used in brackish-water treatment and water reuse. [6]

RO does not eliminate the need for process design. Pretreatment, pressure losses, recovery, energy recovery, cleaning, and brine management affect the overall result. Increasing recovery also increases the concentration of the remaining feed and can raise the required pressure and scaling risk. A membrane’s laboratory rejection value alone cannot establish the efficiency or environmental performance of a desalination plant. [6]

Gas separation and polymer–penetrant interactions

A gas membrane also separates by different transport rates, but it does not necessarily contain pores that behave like a conventional filter. In dense polymers, both gas solubility and molecular mobility influence permeation. Membrane systems are used for carbon-dioxide removal from natural gas, hydrogen recovery from process streams, and nitrogen production from air. The faster-permeating component is enriched on the permeate side, while the slower component is enriched in the retentate. [7]

Material selection depends on the required purity, recovery, pressure and feed composition. Measurements made with a single pure gas may not predict mixed-gas behaviour. Competitive sorption, contaminants, polymer aging and plasticization can change the transport response, so useful comparisons require representative feed and operating conditions. This section describes gas-separation principles within the wider membrane field. [7]

Performance quantities and interpretation

Membrane performance must be expressed using quantities appropriate to the process and driving force. Flux, permeance and rejection describe different aspects of a measurement and should not be used interchangeably. The reported pressure, temperature, feed composition, effective area, conditioning and test duration provide the boundary conditions needed to interpret these quantities. Measurements on selectively coated APS supports illustrate the need to consider both water transport and solute retention. [9]

Common quantities in pressure-driven liquid filtration
QuantityDefinitionInterpretation
Volumetric fluxJv = Vp / (Am Δt)Collected permeate volume divided by effective membrane area and collection time.
Hydraulic permeanceLp = Jv / ΔPPressure-normalized flux for a measurement with negligible opposing osmotic-pressure difference, such as an appropriate pure-water test.
Observed solute rejectionRobs = (1 − Cp / Cf) × 100%Concentration reduction relative to the sampled bulk feed; it depends on the specified sampling and operating conditions.

In these expressions, Vp is permeate volume, Am is effective membrane area, Δt is collection time, ΔP is the transmembrane pressure difference, and Cp and Cf are permeate and bulk-feed concentrations. For an osmotically significant feed, the hydraulic pressure difference alone is not the net thermodynamic driving force. Concentration polarization can also produce a membrane-surface concentration different from the measured bulk value; observed rejection is consequently distinct from a rejection defined using the local interface concentration.

For example, a high clean-water flux does not establish that a membrane will perform well in wastewater. Deposited contaminants can create fouling, a concentrated boundary layer can cause concentration polarization, and pressure can compact the structure. Stable operation, cleaning compatibility, and retention of selectivity are therefore as important as the initial measurement. [1]

Process integration and sustainability

A successful membrane combines an appropriate material with a suitable module and process. Spiral-wound and hollow-fibre modules, for example, package membrane area into workable systems, but their flow conditions and cleaning requirements differ. Scaling up involves controlling defects, maintaining reproducibility, and testing under representative operating conditions.

Sustainable design also considers solvent hazards, water and energy use during fabrication, service life, cleaning chemicals, and end-of-life management. A water-based synthesis or a bio-derived polymer can be valuable, but neither automatically makes the complete system sustainable. These considerations motivate research connecting material chemistry to manufacturing and process operation. [8]

Research

Research overview

Aqueous membrane formation, selective polymer films and interfaces for water separation.

SIM Lab studies aqueous complexation, selective polymer films and membrane surfaces. Its published work connects defined polymer systems and fabrication routes with membrane structure, water transport and solute retention.

Polyelectrolyte complex membranes

Our aqueous phase separation studies include pH-triggered PSS–PAH and PSS–PEI complexation, selective coatings on APS supports, and PSS–PEI hollow fibers. More recent work examines ion-specific effects in salt-triggered PSS–PDADMAC membrane formation. These studies connect polymer ionization or salt exchange with structure development and the measured separation response. Baig et al., 2020–2022; Ahmad et al., 2026.

Thin-film membranes and interfacial chemistry

Published work on polyamide and polyimine thin-film composite membranes examines biobased monomers for brine separation. Earlier thin-film nanocomposite studies address water-vapor transport using functionalized silicon, graphene oxide and GO–TiO₂ additives. These are distinct separation systems with different feed compositions and transport measurements. Baig et al., 2019, 2025.

Surface modification for emulsion separation

The group’s MoS₂ ceramic-membrane study uses polydopamine–tannic acid functionalization to modify wetting and oil adhesion during oil-in-water emulsion treatment. Performance is evaluated through water transport, droplet rejection and recovery after filtration and cleaning. Ahmad et al., 2026.

Research / Methods

Characterization & facilities

Connecting material measurements with membrane behavior.

Membrane characterization is organized around the relationship between a defined preparation history, the resulting material state and its transport response. Specimen conditioning is part of the measurement: a dry cross-section, a hydrated surface and a membrane operating under pressure need not represent the same structure.

Experimental work is supported by SIM Lab and shared KFUPM infrastructure, including characterization access described by the Interdisciplinary Research Center for Membranes and Water Security in collaboration with the Central Research Facilities. The approaches below are grouped by the question they address, rather than presented as an instrument-ownership inventory.

Characterization and fabrication approaches
Research questionApproachesInformation obtained
How does the membrane form?Phase inversion, aqueous phase separation, polyelectrolyte complexation, interfacial polymerization; solution rheologyFabrication–structure relationships and solution behavior
What structure is produced?SEM and AFMMorphology, surface topography and roughness
What chemistry and interface are present?FTIR, XPS, water contact angle and zeta potentialFunctional groups, surface composition, wetting and electrokinetic response
How does it separate?Filtration testing and UV–Vis analysis for suitable solutesWater transport, solute retention and changes during testing

Measurement workflow and data comparability

A characterization sequence should establish the identity and preparation history of a specimen before connecting structural observations to chemical analysis and separation measurements. Where possible, modified and unmodified membranes should be compared using equivalent conditioning, sampling and analysis procedures. The measurements are complementary: surface chemistry does not independently establish pore geometry, and a micrograph does not determine solute selectivity.

Transport experiments require a documented operating boundary condition. Relevant records include membrane orientation and effective area, pressure history, temperature, feed composition, filtration mode and sampling time. Reporting the evolution of transport during conditioning and exposure helps distinguish compaction or fouling from a reproducible difference between membrane formulations.

KFUPM characterization infrastructure ↗

Characterization methods guide

Characterization methods are indexed by their primary analytical purpose. Each entry specifies the observable being measured and the conditions required for a defensible comparison.

9 Methods

Morphology

SEM — scanning electron microscopy

Scanning electron microscopy resolves features of the membrane surface and prepared cross-section. It is used to examine skin continuity, internal morphology and the distribution of visible structural features. Interpretation requires attention to the specimen preparation and imaging conditions: drying, fracture preparation and conductive coating can influence the structure presented to the electron beam.

Report with the result
Specimen preparation, coating, accelerating voltage, magnification and scale bars.
Interpretation note
SEM images show the prepared specimen; they are not a direct measurement of the hydrated pore-size distribution.
Morphology

AFM — atomic force microscopy

Atomic force microscopy measures local surface topography through the interaction of a probe with the sample. Height maps can be analyzed using defined roughness parameters, but the result depends on scan dimensions, probe geometry and data processing. Comparisons are most informative when the same measurement mode, sampling strategy and sample state are maintained.

Report with the result
Scan size, measurement mode, probe information, sample state and roughness convention.
Interpretation note
Compare roughness only at comparable scan sizes and analysis settings.
Technique reference ↗
Chemistry

FTIR — Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy

Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy examines vibrational absorption associated with chemical bonds. In membrane studies, spectra help identify polymer functionalities and changes accompanying modification. Band assignments require chemically appropriate controls, and comparisons must account for sampling mode, background treatment and normalization. A spectral change alone does not uniquely establish the mechanism of a chemical transformation.

Report with the result
Sampling mode, spectral resolution, scan count, background and band assignments.
Interpretation note
A band shift or intensity change should be interpreted with suitable controls, not as standalone proof of a reaction.
Technique reference ↗
Chemistry

XPS — X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy measures the energies of emitted photoelectrons to characterize near-surface elemental composition and chemical environments. Survey spectra and high-resolution regions provide complementary information. Chemical-state assignments depend on charging correction and fitting constraints; the sampled surface can differ in composition from the bulk membrane or from an interface exposed during operation.

Report with the result
Survey and high-resolution spectra, energy calibration, fitting constraints and atomic fractions.
Interpretation note
Surface composition does not necessarily represent the bulk membrane.
Technique reference ↗
Interfaces

Water contact angle

Contact-angle measurements describe the apparent wetting response of a liquid on the measured surface. For porous membranes, the recorded angle may evolve through spreading, absorption or surface reorganization. Droplet volume, observation time and specimen conditioning should therefore accompany the result. Comparisons across different surface roughness or sample states require particular care.

Report with the result
Droplet volume, measurement time, sample conditioning and replicate locations.
Interpretation note
Porosity, roughness and droplet absorption can influence the apparent angle.
Technique reference ↗
Interfaces

Zeta potential

Zeta potential characterizes an electrokinetic response at the membrane–electrolyte interface. It is influenced by the surface, the surrounding solution and the measurement method, rather than being a solution-independent constant. A pH-dependent response can inform the interpretation of interfacial charge behavior when electrolyte identity, concentration, temperature and conditioning are controlled.

Report with the result
Measurement method, electrolyte composition, pH, temperature and conditioning.
Interpretation note
Values depend on solution conditions and should not be treated as an intrinsic constant.
Technique reference ↗
Processing

Rheology

Rheological measurements characterize the flow or viscoelastic response of a membrane-forming formulation. Shear-dependent viscosity and oscillatory measurements address different aspects of solution behavior. Temperature, deformation history, geometry and measurement range determine the meaning of a comparison; these variables are particularly relevant when formulation changes also alter polymer association or solution stability.

Report with the result
Geometry, temperature, shear or frequency range, sample history and replicates.
Interpretation note
Measurements made under different deformation conditions are not directly interchangeable.
Technique reference ↗
Performance

UV–Vis spectroscopy

Ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy measures absorbance and can quantify suitable analytes using a validated calibration. Feed and permeate analysis requires appropriate blanks, a defined wavelength and operation within the calibration range. Matrix effects, scattering and overlapping absorption must be assessed before converting an optical response into a concentration or solute-rejection value.

Report with the result
Wavelength, optical path, blanks, calibration range and dilution factors.
Interpretation note
Concentration estimates require a validated calibration and consideration of interfering species.
Performance

Filtration and separation testing

Filtration experiments couple membrane transport with the hydrodynamic and compositional conditions of the test. Permeate production and feed–permeate analysis must be interpreted with effective area, pressure, temperature and sampling history. Conditioning, compaction, concentration polarization and fouling can change the measured response; their contributions should not be conflated with an intrinsic change in the selective material.

Report with the result
Effective area, pressure, temperature, feed composition, conditioning, sampling times and test configuration.
Interpretation note
Distinguish flux from pressure-normalized permeance, and report how rejection was calculated.

PEC Membrane Database

A searchable literature collection for polyelectrolyte complex membranes prepared by aqueous phase separation.

This initial collection contains five publication-level records. Search by polymer pair, fabrication trigger, membrane geometry or DOI. Each record identifies its source and the scope of the extracted measurements; it does not represent a sample-level experimental dataset.

Permeance is reported in L m⁻² h⁻¹ bar⁻¹ and molecular-weight cut-off (MWCO) in g mol⁻¹. An em dash means the value has not been extracted. Results from different specimen variants and test conditions must be interpreted within the originating paper.

Research article · 2026

Ion-specific effects in PSS–PDADMAC membrane formation

Tausif Ahmad, Nazish Mushtaq, Abdullah Sani and Muhammad Irshad Baig
Journal of Membrane Science · Volume 760 · Article 126240

Salt-shift aqueous phase separation depends on maintaining a processable polymer mixture before inducing complexation during coagulation. The study by Tausif Ahmad, Nazish Mushtaq, Abdullah Sani and Muhammad Irshad Baig examines this problem in a PSS–PDADMAC system by varying the inorganic salt, rather than changing the polymer pair.

Solution stability and exchange behavior

The study reports that some salts produced nonhomogeneous casting solutions through premature association. For the homogeneous formulations, conductivity measurements were used to examine apparent salt release during coagulation. Differences in release behavior were associated with changes in membrane hydration, roughness and internal structure.

Separation response

The measured water permeance increased when NaCl was replaced by KBr, while dye rejection decreased. These results identify a transport–selectivity trade-off within the investigated PSS–PDADMAC formulations. The values below are pressure-normalized permeances, rather than unnormalized water fluxes.

Reported water permeance by salt formulation
Salt formulationWater permeance (L m⁻² h⁻¹ bar⁻¹)
NaCl-based membrane0.99
KBr-based membrane18.29

Design interpretation

The findings distinguish precursor-solution stability from salt exchange during coagulation. In this polymer pair, a suitable salt must first permit homogeneous casting and then support a formation pathway that produces the required transport properties. The observed ordering is specific to the investigated formulations and does not establish a universal salt ranking for PEC membranes.

Salt type as a design parameter for tuning the morphology and separation performance of polyelectrolyte complex membranes prepared by aqueous phase separation

Review article · 2026

Mechanistic framework for aqueous membrane fabrication

Tausif Ahmad, Abdullah Sani and Muhammad Irshad Baig
Desalination · Volume 640 · Article 120712

The review by Tausif Ahmad, Abdullah Sani and Muhammad Irshad Baig examines aqueous phase separation as a membrane-forming process. It relates polymer interactions and aqueous demixing to the structure and separation properties reported in the literature, then considers the engineering requirements for extending these materials beyond laboratory casting.

Polymer ionization and electrostatic screening

pH-triggered and salt-triggered routes change different aspects of a membrane-forming solution. A pH shift alters the charge state of an ionizable polymer, whereas a salinity change modifies electrostatic screening and association between charged chains. The review uses this mechanistic distinction to discuss how a homogeneous precursor develops into a solid membrane.

Separation performance in the reviewed systems

For selected pH-shift systems, the review reports divalent-salt rejection of 94–98% at water permeances of 1.7–4.5 L m⁻² h⁻¹ bar⁻¹. These values summarize published membrane variants; they are not new experimental measurements made in the review. Monovalent-salt retention remains more limited, so pretreatment and softening must be distinguished from stand-alone seawater desalination.

Mechanical and manufacturing constraints

The review identifies mechanical performance, chemical durability and continuous manufacturing as unresolved development requirements. Selective transport on a laboratory specimen does not establish module-scale pressure tolerance or long-term cleaning stability. Its research priorities consequently include network design, durability measurements and production routes capable of maintaining membrane integrity beyond small flat-sheet specimens.

Original publication

Aqueous phase separation membranes: Fundamentals, mechanisms, and emerging green fabrication strategies

Research article · 2026

Polyphenolic engineering of MoS₂ membranes for oily wastewater

Tausif Ahmad, Nadeem Baig, Niaz Ali Khan and Muhammad Irshad Baig
Journal of Membrane Science · Volume 757 · Article 125917

Oil-in-water emulsions present two connected membrane-design problems: retaining dispersed droplets while limiting the accumulation of oil at the separating surface. A study by Tausif Ahmad and co-authors investigates a ceramic-supported molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) membrane whose surface chemistry is modified with polydopamine and tannic acid (PDA–TA). The work examines how this modification affects the interface encountered by an aqueous emulsion.

Surface modification and membrane architecture

The reported functionalization improves nanosheet processing, adhesion and water affinity while retaining the underlying MoS₂ crystal structure. A 10 mg loading of functionalized material produces the separating layer discussed in the study. Its underwater oil contact angle is approximately 150°, consistent with an interface that resists oil wetting when immersed in water.

Reported separation and cleaning response

The measurements below describe different experiments. Pure-water flux characterizes transport before an oil-containing feed is introduced; oil rejection describes emulsion separation, and flux recovery measures performance following the reported filtration and cleaning cycles.

Selected results reported in the paper
MeasurementReported resultExperimental context
Pure-water flux714 L m⁻² h⁻¹At 0.5 bar; reported for the functionalized membrane
Oil-droplet rejection>97%Surfactant-stabilized oil-in-water emulsions; at 0.5 bar
Flux recovery ratio83%Following cyclic filtration and hydraulic cleaning

The authors associate the separation response with the laminar MoS₂ structure and the hydrated PDA–TA interface. This interpretation links access to water-transport pathways with reduced adhesion of oil at the membrane surface.

Interpretation for oily-water treatment

For process evaluation, the distinction between these observables is essential. A clean-water flux cannot be substituted for the sustained production rate during emulsion filtration. Similarly, a flux recovery ratio describes the response to a particular exposure and cleaning procedure; it is not a measure of complete oil removal or an independent prediction of service life.

The study therefore provides a material-specific demonstration of interfacial modification for emulsion treatment. Applying this approach to another wastewater requires comparison of droplet size, surfactant composition, aqueous chemistry and operating history. Such comparisons establish whether the observed wetting and fouling response is retained under the conditions of the proposed application.

Original publication

Polyphenolic engineering of MoS₂ ceramic membranes for oily wastewater separation

Biography

Dr Muhammad Irshad Baig is the Principal Investigator of SIM Lab and an Assistant Professor at KFUPM. His research concerns aqueous phase separation, polyelectrolyte complex membranes and thin-film composite materials. He joined KFUPM in August 2024 after postdoctoral appointments at the University of Twente and KAUST.

His doctoral research at Twente examined sustainable polyelectrolyte complex membranes produced through aqueous phase separation. His current research interests include membrane fabrication, interfacial polymerization, surface modification and the relationship between material chemistry and separation performance.
